summary: One of a series of periodic snapshots of which protocols were standards and what stage each had reached, as tracked by the IAB. It is historic now, because later editions in the series replaced it, and it was replaced by RFC 2200.

eli5.summary: It is an old report card listing which Internet rules were officially approved at the time. Newer report cards replaced it.

questions: what was the internet official protocol standards list
which protocols were standards in the 1990s
how often was the standards list updated
subtitle: A snapshot of protocol standardization status in early 1997

tldr.problem: Internet standards evolve continuously, and operators need up-to-date information on which protocols are approved, in testing, or obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2000 is a periodic snapshot of the standardization status of all Internet protocols, categorized by maturity level (standard through historic) and requirement level (required through not recommended), following the same model as its predecessors.
tldr.outcome: This was replaced by RFC 2200 as the periodic standards list. RFC 2000 is now historic.

today: RFC 2200 replaced this document, which is now historic. RFC 2000 was a snapshot of Internet standards as of February 1997.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2000 describes the current state of standardization for Internet protocols as of February 1997. Like its predecessor RFC 1880, it is one of a series of periodic snapshots maintained by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB).

This edition obsoletes RFC 1920 from late 1996 and represents the state of standards after approximately one year of protocol development. The document covers the same taxonomy and process as RFC 1880: two-dimensional protocol classification by maturity level and requirement level, the standardization track, and comprehensive lists of all significant Internet protocols.
sections.eli5: This is an updated version of the standards report from about a year before. It shows the same information in the same way, but with newer protocols and updated statuses.

sections.title: Standardization Levels and Categories
sections.content:
Protocols are classified on two independent axes. Maturity levels (or states) range from Standard (official) through Draft Standard and Proposed Standard, to Experimental, Informational, and Historic (no longer in use). Requirement levels (or statuses) indicate whether a protocol is Required (must implement), Recommended (should implement), Elective (optional), Limited Use (special circumstances only), or Not Recommended (should not use).

When a protocol enters the standards track as a Proposed Standard, the IESG also decides its eventual requirement level. Protocols must remain at each level for a minimum time before advancement: at least 6 months as Proposed Standard, at least 4 months as Draft Standard. Advancement from Draft Standard to Standard requires demonstrated operational experience and interoperability of at least two independent implementations.
sections.eli5: Every protocol gets two grades. One shows how tested and approved it is. The other shows whether it is required, optional, or not recommended.

sections.title: The IETF, IESG, and Standards Organizations
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is the primary body developing Internet standards. It operates through working groups and is overseen by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). The Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) manages research-level work. The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) provides overall guidance and charter review.

Standards documents (those designated Standard, Draft Standard, or Proposed Standard) must receive explicit IESG approval before publication. Experimental documents are notified to the IESG but may be published at the RFC Editor's discretion. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) manages the protocol registry and assigned numbers.
sections.eli5: Different committees make decisions about protocols. The main committee (IETF) decides which protocols should be standards. Other groups review and approve the decisions.

sections.title: The Standards Track and Protocol Evolution
sections.content:
New protocols begin at state 0 (entry point) and may follow different paths. Protocols intended for standardization enter as Proposed Standards (state 1). After 6 months and community review, they may advance to Draft Standard (state 2). After 4 more months and successful implementation experience, they reach Standard (state 3), receiving an STD number.

Some protocols may be directed to Experimental (state 4) status for research purposes and remain there indefinitely. Others may be moved to Historic (state 5) when superseded or when no longer suitable for general use. The document notes that the minimum time periods (6 months for Proposed, 4 months for Draft) are enforced to allow adequate community review and testing.
sections.eli5: New protocols start at the bottom and move up through several approval levels. Each level requires tests and time. Some protocols are only for experiments and never become official standards.

sections.title: Standard Protocols and Reference Documents
sections.content:
RFC 2000 lists hundreds of protocols across all categories. Standard Protocols (such as TCP, IP, UDP, SMTP, FTP, and DNS) are listed first with their requirement levels. Network-Specific Standard Protocols (for various link types and media) follow. The Telnet Options are catalogued separately with individual status entries.

The document references three key companion specifications: Assigned Numbers (RFC 1700), which defines protocol parameter values; Host Requirements (RFCs 1122 and 1123), which specify mandatory and elective features for Internet hosts; and Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers (RFC 1812), which does the same for routers. These documents provide implementation details not covered in the standards list itself.
sections.eli5: The document lists all the protocols, sorted by how approved they are. It also points to other documents that explain the details of how each protocol works.
